newsitem.title: INDIA: India wheat product exports grind to a halt.
newsitem.headline: India wheat product exports grind to a halt.

text.p: Indian exports of wheat products have ground to a standstill as foreign sales have reached a 150,000-tonne limit, traders and analysts said on Tuesday.
"The cieling was exhausted by November," said one Bombay-based commodity analyst who asked not to be identified.
"After that, no additional quantities have been released. So in effect, there are no wheat product exports currently from India."
The Commerce Ministry in October amended its export policy to impose a ceiling of 150,000 tonnes on exports of wheat products. The ceiling will remain in effect until the end of March, 1997.
The ministry introduced the change in its five-year export-import policy that covers the period up to March 31, 1997, to ensure domestic availability of wheat.

Earlier, India halted wheat exports after the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), which handles wheat exports, stopped issuing export permits to check domestic prices and augument domestic supplies.
"I don't think any new quotas (for wheat products exports) will be released," said Tarun Kumar of Space Group, a leading Delhi foodgrains exporter.
"Our buffer stocks are not as strong as last year," Kumar said.
As of November 1, the state-run Food Corporation of India (FCI) held 9.54 million tonnes of wheat. Comparative figures for November 1995 were not available.
On October 1, FCI held 19.7 million tonnes of foodgrains -- which includes wheat, rice and various cereals -- down drastically from 29.9 million tonnes a year earlier.
Traders said a fall in government reserves had prompted wheat prices to rise in recent months by about 20 percent compared with prices a year ago.
They said traders were hoarding stocks, expecting to sell later when the government would authorise wheat product exports.
"(Wheat) prices have gone up because of speculation and hoarding," said one Delhi-based foodgrains exporter.
"People think they will be allowed to export later," he said.
